Thirty-one percent to six percent, on the same model.

Nobody rebuilt it. The formulas that produced a 31 percent error on net burn
in Q1 produced a 6 percent error two quarters later, unchanged. What changed
was the two paragraphs above the table.

You will say the model was wrong. It was not, particularly. It was reporting
a number nobody in the room had agreed to read the same way, so every month
the board argued about the definition and nobody argued about the plan.

So we wrote down what net burn meant here. One sentence, in the pack, above
the number. Cash out minus cash in, capitalised salaries included, one time
items named separately and never netted. Six weeks later the error had not
moved. Four months later it had, because people had started forecasting the
thing the sentence described instead of the thing they each assumed.

The model was never the artefact. The sentence above it was.

If your forecast error is not coming down, do not open the spreadsheet. Open
the last three board packs and read only the commentary. Count how many
different things the same word is doing.

Then pick one and write it down.

Nadia Feriel, fractional CFO for seed and Series A B2B SaaS.
I build the model and I sit in the room when it gets argued about.
